findings.title: Email validation mutates DB causing double-counted block stats
findings.body: EmailValidator.validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count, updates last_match_at and saves. Validation is supposed to be side-effect free. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, each of which runs validations, so a single blocked signup attempt increments the counter twice. Any other call to valid? (admin UI, console, tests) also mutates stats even if the user is never saved. Consequence is inflated match_count and misleading last_match_at, making abuse metrics unreliable.

findings.title: Non-atomic match_count increment loses concurrent updates
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does read-modify-write: record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save. Concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can interleave reads and overwrite each other, losing increments. The save also runs full validations including an extra uniqueness SELECT. Consequence is lost counts under load and wasted queries. Should use an atomic increment such as increment_counter or update_counters that bypasses validations.

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive allowing bypass
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up with BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first using the raw user-supplied string with no downcasing or stripping, and the model validates uniqueness case-sensitively. Email delivery treats addresses case-insensitively in practice and users can add case changes or whitespace. An attacker blocked as bad@spam.com can sign up as BAD@spam.com or Bad@spam.com and miss the block, and admins can create logically duplicate block entries. Should normalize emails on save and lookup, e.g. with Email.downcase and strip.

findings.title: change_email action bypasses blocked-email check
findings.body: UsersController#change_email lowercases the new address, checks only whether another User already owns it, then creates an EmailToken and enqueues authorization without ever running EmailValidator or checking BlockedEmail.should_block?. An address rejected at signup as blocked can therefore still be adopted by an existing account via the email-change flow. Consequence is the blocklist is ineffective after account creation. The new address should be validated the same way as signup.

findings.title: Wrong Ember dependent key prevents rejected-email UI update
findings.body: emailValidation is declared dependent on accountEmail and rejectedEmails.@each. In Ember, @each observes properties of array items, not array membership; pushing a string with pushObject does not invalidate the computed property. The correct key is rejectedEmails.[] or length. After the server rejects an email and it is pushed into rejectedEmails, the validation still returns ok and submitDisabled stays false until the user edits the email, so the user can immediately resubmit the same blocked email repeatedly.

findings.title: Shared mutable rejectedEmails array on prototype
findings.body: CreateAccountController is extended with rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) as a prototype property. That single array instance is shared by all instances of the controller. Pushes of server-rejected emails leak across modal instances and persist after close/reopen, causing stale addresses to be treated as rejected for future unrelated signups. Mutable defaults should be created per-instance in init or reset when the modal opens.

findings.title: Domain whitelist regex not anchored allows subdomain spoof
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(domains)") with no end anchor and matches by substring. A whitelist entry like example.com therefore matches user@example.com.evil.com because the string contains @example.com, even though the real domain is evil.com. The whitelisted user passes validation incorrectly. Similarly a blacklist can over-match. The regex should be anchored to the end of the address and handle domain boundaries correctly.
